chapter_theme: General songs (பொதுப்பாடல்கள், 16 of 21): confessions of courtesans who price love, of praising patrons and of wealth hoarded without sharing, the funeral and the rotting body, set against pleas for the feet, for Saiva knowledge of Lord, soul and bond, and in 1221 the poet's disowning of every act as his own.
structure_note: The general songs run in order of their first letter (இ, உ, ஊ, எ, ஏ, க). Courtesans and price: 1229 to 1231; women's eyes and infatuation: 1217, 1218, 1223, 1225, 1228; the poet's trade of praising patrons: 1224, 1226, 1231; the funeral: 1227. 1219 and 1221 are doctrinal, and 1222 sets the mantra against Death's servants.

1217.reading: The poet confesses his enjoyment of slender-waisted women, their lips and camphor-smeared breasts, and asks for even a little grace so that, his base qualities gone through awareness of the attributeless, he may enter the one partless form. The praise tells of Brahma thrown into prison, names Vishnu as eater of curd, ghee and the world and brother-in-law of Siva who ate the poison, and calls Murugan the victor whose vel struck the gods' foes and felled the eight mountains.
1217.nuance: நிற்குண உணர்வாலே ஒரு நிஷ்கள வடிவில் புக: the goal is put in Sanskrit doctrinal terms, entry into the nirguna, nishkala form, against the துற்குணம் of the first lines. Brahma's imprisonment is named without its cause. The run of lines 5 to 7 (who fears whom) is hard to divide.

1218.reading: The poet describes women's dark eyes that leap to the earrings, roam in the hair's shade, speak the Veda of love and strike like spears and poison, and asks that he, who withered in their embrace, be set on the way by having Pati, pasu and pasam separated each from each without stain. The praise names Rama who went with the monkeys and felled the ten crowns with one arrow, calls Murugan the teacher whose instruction ash-adorned Siva understood, Valli's lord, the one who resettled Indra, and lord of yogis rapt in jnana.
1218.nuance: பதி பசு பாசம் ஆனவை கசடற வேறு வேறு செய்தருள்வாயே: the plea is in the terms of Saiva Siddhanta, asking for the discrimination of Lord, soul and bond. The praise has விபூதி பூஷணர் உணர் உபதேச தேசிக, Siva learning from Murugan, without naming Om.

1219.reading: The poet asks Murugan to drive off his twofold disease of impurity with Siva's light, call him kindly, set the paired feet on his head, seat him on the peacock, give him the vel, and grant him the place of a teacher whom the Vedas, gods and earth would praise. The praise calls Murugan younger brother of the elephant-faced god who cuts the disease of birth and poverty, wearer of kadamba, embracer of the wise wife Vishnu gave, and the one who powdered the hill, cut down the asuras and freed the gods.
1219.nuance: The plea is unusually bold: not only the feet on the head (முடிமேலே இணைதாள்) but the peacock, the vel and உபதேசிகப் பதம், the rank of a teacher. இருவோரும் ஒருவாக, 'the two as one', given by the lord of Kailasa, is obscure; it may mean Siva and Uma joined. Ganapati is praised at length in the second half.

1220.reading: The poet asks whether his mind will not think day and night on the feet with little anklet bells that prattle the Vedas, adorned with the lotus of his heart and with flowers, and whether Murugan will not take pity on a deceiver with no help but his grace, who carries a body of five elements from world to world. The praise is of battle, an elephant and the golden hill, the sea set on fire, and Siva and Uma praising the child Kandan while all worlds, gods, Vishnu and Brahma bow.
1220.nuance: பஞ்சபூத உடலது சுமந்து அலைந்து உலகுதொறும் வந்துவந்து: rebirth is told as carrying the five-element body from world to world. The poet calls himself வஞ்சகன், a deceiver. The battle lines (கனநிவத... கடகசயிலம்) are hard to divide.

1221.reading: The poet calls his body flesh, bone, filth and nerves, eaten by fated disease, and himself the lowest dog, and asks who he is to subside, to bow, to sing Murugan in joy, to melt, to wither, to walk and fall. The praise answers with Siva, who himself united, knew, rejoiced, pitied like a mother, became Siva, grew and remained by himself, and calls Murugan his son and lord of the devotees of salokam, samipam and sarupam.
1221.nuance: The repeated நானார் ('who am I') is set against the repeated தானே ('he himself'): the poet disowns every act of devotion as his own and gives all agency to the Lord who does everything by himself. The three devotee classes in the refrain are the graded releases short of union; sayujyam is not named. The word after மகிழ்ந்து in line 10 is garbled.

1222.reading: The poet asks whether he will worship the red feet adorned with kadamba, jasmine, kuvalai and vetchi, having won manhood by cutting down with the sword of mantra, which the sects, rites and all sixty-four arts cannot reach, the cruel servants of Yama who come by fate's path to take his life, and which those who wander raising banners that say none is their equal never find. The praise calls Murugan the red-handed vel that fought Diti's sons and bathed in a river of blood, rider of the bright peacock, and lord of the thirty-three gods, which it counts out.
1222.nuance: மந்த்ர வாளால் ... யமபடரை வெட்டித் துணித்து: the mantra is a sword against Death's servants, and it lies beyond the boasting sects and arts. The refrain lists the thirty-three: eleven on bulls (the Rudras), twelve in chariots (the Adityas), two Ashvins and eight Vasus. The opening lines' split is uncertain.

1223.reading: The poet asks whether he must wander, worn out with a heart sore and burning, after women whose young-coconut breasts draw young men's eyes, who cling with love and then leave without attachment by deceit. The praise calls Murugan younger brother of the pot-bellied elephant god who gathers fruit, sugarcane and cakes in his trunk and is kind to devotees, and the beautiful one whose vel split the sea and pursued and cut down the great mango.
1223.nuance: அணைந்து பின் பற்றற்று அகல் மாயம்: the deceit is the women's leaving once attached, not a price named. கொக்கு is the mango, the form Sura took, a detail the song names by its word only.

1224.reading: The poet asks whether his dying will not end: a body for crows, dogs, jackals and ghosts, whether in forest, country or house, after seeking what is sweet in writings and songs, piling great wealth and eating it without sharing, and boasting of high lineage. The praise names Murugan lord of the daughter of thousand-eyed Indra, the peacock-rider whose vel fought Sura, the Vel of Kongu, partner of the hunters' girl, and lord of the gods who offer flowers at his feet.
1224.nuance: பாத்து உணாது: eating without dividing it with others, the Kural's own phrase for sharing, here named as the poet's fault. கொங்கில் வேளே places the song in Kongu without naming a shrine. The opening search in ஏட்டிலே ... பாட்டிலே ... நீட்டிலே may be of a poet's trade; its sense is uncertain.

1225.reading: The poet asks whether, infatuated by bodiced breasts and red-veined carp eyes that spit poison like Death, he should go about without fear or shame, called a rake by all who hear, mad after wealth. The praise is a dense string of epithets naming the green dancer, the one who dwells in the lotus, the bearer of the discus and conch and the gods of the sky, and calls Murugan the one who cut down the great mango in the sea.
1225.nuance: அச்சக் கூச்சமற்று ... தூர்த்தன் என: the confession is of public shame, being named a rake (தூர்த்தன்). The praise's clipped syllables are very hard to divide and only its last line is clear.

1226.reading: The poet confesses stealing the old poets' phrases (eyes bigger than the sea, breasts bigger than mountains, lips redder than coral, shoulders softer than bamboo) and singing them on a man, calling him strong, peerless, gracious and fearless in hope of gain, and says 'enough, enough' of this restless birth, asking for the red lotus feet. The praise likens the must of the white elephant to two rivers falling from the silver mountain, and calls Murugan the one who took the vel so Indra and the worlds might stand, set the sea crying for refuge and fought the asuras with the hill.
1226.nuance: பழங் கிளவி பல களவுகொண்டு: the poet calls his borrowed stock comparisons theft, and the praise of a patron (அடல் அசஞ்சலன் அதுலன் அநுபமன்) begging. அலமலம், 'enough, enough', turns from the patron to the feet.

1227.reading: The poet describes the funeral: drums beat, young men of the clan bind the body, wrap it in a torn cloth on the bier, burn it, bathe and go home to sit, and says life is pure falsehood; he asks for the high state of Siva so that sorrowful birth may go. The praise calls Murugan the vel that bored through the eight mountains and eased the gods, the one who beguiled the hill girl and embraced her, wearer of kadamba and vetchi, and the one who cut down his foe in the sea.
1227.nuance: சுத்தப் பொய் ஒப்பது உயிர்வாழ்வு: the funeral is told without comment until this judgement. மிக்கச் சிவத்ததொரு சொர்க்கப் பதம் may mean 'a heavenly state that is wholly Siva' or 'very red', a pun on சிவம்.

1228.reading: The poet asks whether the illusion in which his heart goes and dies in the deceitful love of women, sweet-spoken, bee-haired, carp-eyed and moon-faced, will not end. The praise calls Murugan the one who went with love to the hill where the cloud-haired, cuckoo-voiced hill girl lives, who made Sura's sea boil, and who conquered both maya and Kama.
1228.nuance: வென்று மாயையும் அன்றி வேளையும் வென்று: in the refrain Murugan conquers maya and Vel (Kama), so the praise answers the plea's மாயம். The source has யாயை, read as மாயை; the reading is tentative.

1229.reading: The poet describes women who leave men with a begging bowl, catch young men with kohl-eyes, stained teeth and painted faces, and asks whether it is not enough, now that he who clung to them has suffered, to be set at the lotus feet. The praise calls Murugan one who was born as a child to a line it names and removed a fault, the one who meets the breasts of the creeper girl born of the deer to the Brahmin sage, and who crushed the seven hills with his arms.
1229.nuance: கப்பரை கைக்கொள வைப்பவர்: the women reduce men to the beggar's bowl, so the loss of wealth is named in the first words. The lines on முத்தரையர்க்கு ஒரு மகவாகி point to a birth story I cannot identify; they may allude to Murugan as a saint, but the text does not say.

1230.reading: The poet asks for the red feet, praised by the ancient Veda and adorned with jasmine and kuravam, while life lasts in a body that wilts among women who show their price and men of false learning and liquor. The praise calls Murugan the child who longed for the breasts of the parrot girl guarding millet, the peacock hero who freed the prisoners, the vel that felled the mountain, and the good lord of devotees who crown his feet with lilies.
1230.nuance: விலை காட்டு ... அரிவைமார்: the women show a price. Most of the first four lines, in a clipped rhyme on -ல்ல, are hard to divide, so the company the poet lists is uncertain.

1231.reading: The poet says some sell the pleasure of love after reckoning the coins in a man's hand, and some learn and make poems on these women's limbs; he asks whether it would be shameful if he forgot such speech, knew Murugan as the true, sang 'refuge' to his musk-scented feet and melted. The praise names Rama, who with Sugriva's army raised dust from the sea, burned Lanka and shot the one arrow at ten-headed Ravana, as Murugan's uncle, and tells of Murugan taking a hunter's form, mad with love, to find Valli in the hills.
1231.nuance: கைக்காசின் அளவறிந்து: the price is measured to the coin. The poet sets two trades side by side, the women who sell love and the poets who sing their bodies, and offers his song to the feet instead.

links.note: Both follow the corpse from the house: the kin strip him or wrap him in torn cloth, light the pyre and then bathe. The Tirumanthiram calls them people without justice; 1227 calls life itself pure falsehood and asks for the state of Siva.

The Kural's women who weigh the profit before they speak match 1231's women who sell love after reckoning the coins in a man's hand (கைக்காசின் அளவறிந்து); 1231 adds the poets who sing such women's bodies.
Both confess the court poet's sin of singing a patron in borrowed praise for gain; 1226 calls the stock comparisons stolen, 1022 the patron undeserving, and both turn the song to the feet.
Tirumular explains salokam, samipam and sarupam as stages gained through chariyai and the paths after it; 1221 names Murugan lord of the devotees of exactly these three, stopping short of sayujyam.

source_issues: 1221: line 10 is garbled (மகிழ்ந்து ...... அ ளுறித்), with initial அ split from its word.
1228: யாயையு in line 15 is probably மாயையு.
1231: ஡ is corrupt three times: சுக்஡ணவ and தசக்஡ணவ for சுக்ரீவ and தசக்ரீவ (஡ண for ரீ), and கடற்று஡ளி for கடல் தூளி (஡ for ஊ).
1217, 1218, 1219, 1220, 1221, 1231: initial உ is split from its word by a space (உ டன்மற்கடை, உ ணருப, உ பதேசி, உ னதருளை, உ டலது, உ னையோத, உ ளநெ, உ பய).
